paras: The attempted lynching of Grant Holly took place in Nevada County, Arkansas, in about June 1888, when armed men and gathered citizens tried to seize a Black man accused of attempting to assault a white woman near Bowden. The sheriff moved Holly to the state penitentiary at Little Rock for safe-keeping, and in November a deputy took him back to Prescott for trial.

Holly, described as "colored" and "a negro," was charged with attempting "to outrage a respectable white lady" at a small town on the Iron Mountain Railroad, which the Osceola Times placed near Bowden. Neither account names the woman or gives Holly's version.

According to a Little Rock dispatch, "a large number of citizens gathered" at the time of the alleged attempt, and their "frequent threats of lynching" led the sheriff to take the prisoner away. The Osceola Times reported that several attempts were made to mob Holly. As the train carrying him passed Bowden, six armed men tried to board it to "secure their man," but the conductor held them off until he could start the train. Sheriff J. S. Reagan of Nevada County then lodged Holly in the penitentiary at Little Rock.

Holly stayed in the penitentiary until November 7, 1888, when Deputy Sheriff J. B. Crossland came up from Prescott and took him back for trial in the Nevada County Circuit Court that week. No report of the trial or its outcome was found, and no arrest of the armed men or of anyone who threatened Holly is reported.

Coverage was brief and appeared only in the white press. The Osceola Times ran the episode in early July as one item in its "Arkansas State News" column, stating the alleged assault as fact and reporting the mob attempts without comment. Four months later the Memphis Appeal printed a special dispatch from Little Rock under the headline "A Rapist Taken Back," with the subhead "Great Fears of Lynching," calling Holly a rapist although the charge was attempted outrage. Neither paper criticized the would-be lynchers; both treated the sheriff's removal of the prisoner as the newsworthy point.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Grant Holly
bases: Armed men and gathered citizens tried to seize and threatened to lynch Grant Holly, a Black prisoner accused of attempted assault, who was moved to the penitentiary to prevent it (A1, A2).

Six armed men and a gathering of citizens tried to seize Holly and threatened to lynch him over an accusation of attempted assault on a white woman, but he was moved to safety and no one was killed (A1, A2); this was an attempted lynching.

A state-news item in the Osceola Times (A1) and a separate Little Rock dispatch to the Memphis Appeal four months later (A2) agree that Holly was lodged in the Little Rock penitentiary to save him from a lynch mob.

accounts.label: Arkansas state news column
accounts.gist: Holly, accused of attempting to assault a white woman near Bowden, was the target of several attempts to mob him; six armed men tried to board his train at Bowden but the conductor held them off, and the sheriff lodged him in the penitentiary.

accounts.label: Little Rock special dispatch
accounts.gist: When the alleged attempt occurred, a large crowd of citizens gathered and made frequent lynching threats, so the sheriff took Holly to Little Rock in June; in November a deputy took him back for trial.

framing.detail: A short item in a state-news column that reports the mob attempts without comment and states the alleged assault as fact ('who attempted an assault upon a white woman').

Headlined 'A RAPIST TAKEN BACK / To Stand His Trial—Great Fears of Lynching', the dispatch called Holly a rapist before trial while noting that the charge was attempted outrage; it did not comment on the lynching threats.
